name: Bafou
autonymMeaning: “those who dig down to the bottom”, who go in depth
overview: The majority and largely indigenous people of the Menoua, neighbouring Baleveng, Bafoussam and Mbouda, the Bafou speak Yemba. The chiefdom relies on the colleges of the “9” and the “7” notables, ritual societies and a rich skull cult; farming, livestock and trade sustain the community, which celebrates its Lemou festival every two years.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, relatively homogeneous and made up mostly of indigenous people, in contact with Baleveng, Bafoussam and Mbouda.
Yemba is spoken there in its Bafou-North variety, specific to the grouping.
Women and men alike readily marry into other groupings.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Bafou occupy their ancestral land; their name evokes those who get to the bottom of things.
The founder came from Baleveng, with no intermediate stopover. Ties with Baleveng lasted for a time, then loosened.
The split goes back to a conflict between the founder and his brother, chief of Baleveng: history keeps the trace of it.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Society is organised around age classes, castes and the colleges of the 9 and the 7 notables.
The notables deliberate among themselves then decide with the chief, who then gathers the people to announce the decision.
Hierarchy of speech: unmarried men do not speak in front of married men, women keep silent in the presence of men, and elites and brave men are listened to most.
Names and titles are inherited within one's clan (madzong); one cannot inherit from another clan.

Permanent ritual societies: the mothers of twins (magni), who consecrate twins and support new mothers; the ŋkem metem wa'a, the only ones admitted to sacred places to intercede with the ancestors; the ŋkem ŋgya nzɛhɛ, in charge of purifying the village.
Deference: one stops to let the chief pass; an uninitiated boy never sits on the traditional three-legged chair.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; after the bride price, the wife joins her in-laws.
A boy becomes a man by entering his grouping (madzong); a girl becomes a woman at puberty.
Ages given: about 21 for the man, 18 for the woman.
Steps: choice and consent of the betrothed, meeting of the families, negotiations, consultation of the ancestors (methō mpfhō), then bride price.
The bride price comprises a hoe, a blanket, entry fees (ŋkǒ ŋgyā), seating fees (naŋa sī), the hand-washing rite (esōk mbu), dishes, gifts and raw foodstuffs.
Symbols: kola nut and white wine seal the pact like an alliance; earth taken from the skulls of the ancestors brings blessing and protection; the jujube tree means protection and peace.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The skull cult (pah methō mpfō) is at the heart of religious life, together with the traditional tribunal (fə̄m) and the societies ŋgyā ndə́m and ŋkāŋ.
Sacred places: Ndzi'mpfəŋ (in Ndzi'i), Efɔ mə́ŋ lepɛ́ (Balepeh), Efɔ ntoo lefok (Lefok), ŋkuŋkuŋ nda laa (Saa Maya), Nzəm laa (Bameleu), Efɔ shwihi (Ndzenkap).
These sites recall natural phenomena, a hot spring that appeared after a sacrifice, a cave used as a refuge during the maquis, or a mythical snake with a goatee and a crest.
Birth may mark the return of an ancestor; death takes one back to the ancestors. The living consult them in sacred places in case of serious difficulty.
Taboos: incest (sǒk kihi), relations with the wife of the chief or of a notable, murder, adultery, theft, and even eating taro other than with the fingers.
Capital offences punished by banishment: murder, adultery; theft could mean banishment or death. It is also forbidden to curse in a sacred place or to use mystical power to harm.
Divination: diviners, signs given by animals, strange phenomena, dreams and visionaries.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade and chair carving. Women: farming and running the home.
The land goes to the first occupant; it is accessed by gift, through the father, by succession, purchase or inheritance.
Ancestral crafts: hunting and war arrows (mekɔŋɔ), knives (pu'), machetes (nyi), axes (ndza), throwing weapons (eshua') and dance masks.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Traditional nzhó le khʉ attire for men and women alike, with wrappers.
Massive recourse to traditional healers, seers and diviners, both for health and to appease the spirits.
Beauty: the robust, tall, muscular, good-humoured man; the full-figured, well-styled and well-groomed woman.
Courtship: the man strong, protective, well placed socially; the woman hard-working, a good cook, singer and dancer.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances and instruments: ŋgu'efɔ (large and small drum) for funerals in the presence of the chief and the festival; samba for rejoicing and the bride price; akɔ'ndzaŋ for mourning; kwákwá for meetings and twin ceremonies; ku'ŋgaŋ for funerals and the coming out of the chief of the la'akam; kúkho for women's meetings.
Instruments: drums, bell (azə̄ŋ), rattles, whistles, castanets, tam-tam.
Festival: the Lemou festival, every two years in November, and the anniversary of the chief's enthronement every year.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The founder, Tɛla' (“the father of the forge”), was renamed Efɔ ndɔŋ (“the chief of the horns”) after killing a buffalo and refusing to give its head to the chiefdom of Baleveng.

sections.title: The names
items: Names follow circumstances: Nkenfack designates the child born after twins; one also finds Ndonfack, Fouefack, Lemofack, Sofack.
The name evokes a happy or unhappy event, a friendship or a namesake.
One changes name only once: at ennoblement, for recognised qualities or after the birth of twins.
Appellatives and titles: ndzi, ŋkem, tɛnyi, mɔ́'ɔ.

lessons.title: Who are the Bafou? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bafou community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bafou community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bafou community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bafou community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bafou community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bafou call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, relatively homogeneous and made up mainly of indigenous people, in contact with Baleveng, Bafoussam and Mbouda. • Yemba is spoken there in its Bafou-Nord variety, specific to the grouping. • Women and men alike readily marry in other groupings. • The Bafou occupy their ancestral land; their name evokes those who get to the bottom of things. • The founder came from Baleveng, with no intermediate stage. Ties with Baleveng lasted for a time, then loosened.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The majority and largely indigenous people of the Menoua, neighbouring Baleveng, Bafoussam and Mbouda, the Bafou speak Yemba. The chiefdom relies on the colleges of the “9” and the “7” notables, ritual societies and a rich skull cult; farming, livestock and trade sustain the community, which celebrates its Lemou festival every two years.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bafou community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bafou
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bafou organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Bafou village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bafou organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Bafou village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Society is organised in age classes, castes and around the colleges of the 9 and the 7 notables. • The notables deliberate among themselves, then decide with the chief, who then gathers the people to announce the decision. • Hierarchy of speech: unmarried men do not speak in front of married men, women stay silent in the presence of men, and elites and brave men are listened to most. • Names and titles are inherited within one's own clan (madzong); one cannot inherit from another clan. • Permanent ritual societies: the mothers of twins (magni), who consecrate twins and guide new mothers; the ŋkem metem wa'a, the only ones admitted to sacred places to intercede with the ancestors; the ŋkem ŋgya nzɛhɛ, in charge of the village's purifications.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Bafou, then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bafou
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bafou, describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bafou.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bafou, describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bafou.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: taro in yellow sauce (apā na'nū), akəndɔŋ mbap, boiled maize (ŋgəsaŋ mesnə̄k), pounded macabo with greens (akwaa ndzap). • Drinks: raffia wine, palm wine, maize wine. • Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade and chair carving. Women: farming and running the home. • Ancestral crafts: hunting and war arrows (mekɔŋɔ), knives (pu'), machetes (nyi), axes (ndza), throwing weapons (eshua') and dance masks.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bafou mainly eat taro in yellow sauce, akəndɔŋ mbap, ŋgəsaŋ mesnə̄k, pounded macabo with vegetables. Traditional drinks: raffia wine, palm wine, maize wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bafou: write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Clothing, adornments and crafts of the Bafou

objectives: Identify craft objects and their use

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How did people dress in the past, and how do they dress today? — Do clothes indicate status or occasion? — What objects are made, from what materials, and for what uses? — What are the criteria of beauty?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Bafou
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Bafou marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Bafou woman. What steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Bafou marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Bafou woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: Patrilineal kinship; after the bride price, the wife joins her in-laws. Stages: choice and consent of the fiancés, meeting of the families, negotiations, consultation of the ancestors (methō mpfhō), then bride price.

steps.instruction: In a group, act out a marriage proposal among the Bafou, then explain the meaning of two elements of the bride price.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Bafou
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Bafou, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Bafou dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Bafou, choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Bafou dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Dances and instruments: ŋgu'efɔ (large and small drum) for funerals in the presence of the chief and the festival; samba for celebrations and the bride price; akɔ'ndzaŋ for mourning; kwákwá for gatherings and twin ceremonies; ku'ŋgaŋ for funerals and when the chief of the la'akam comes out; kúkho for women's gatherings. • Instruments: drums, bell (azə̄ŋ), rattles, whistles, castanets, tam-tam. • Festival: the Lemou festival, every two years in November, and the anniversary of the chief's enthronement every year.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Bafou, traditional dances (ŋgu'efɔ, rejoicing, bride price, twin ceremonies) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drums, azə̄ŋ bell, rattles, castanets. Festival(s): Lemou festival, anniversary of the chief's enthronement.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Bafou dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bafou
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bafou, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bafou. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bafou, the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bafou. First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, livestock, trade and chair carving. Women: farming and running the home. • Land goes to the first occupant; it is obtained by gift, from the father, by succession, purchase or inheritance. • Ancestral crafts: hunting and war arrows (mekɔŋɔ), knives (pu'), machetes (nyi), axes (ndza), throwing weapons (eshua') and dance masks.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade and chair carving. Women: farming and running the home. Land goes to the first occupant; it is accessed by gift, through the father, by succession, purchase or inheritance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bafou's activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade and chair carving. Women: farming and running the home. Land goes to the first occupant; it is accessed by gift, through the father, by succession, purchase or inheritance.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bafou
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: manger le taro avec une fourchette

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bafou, and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bafou. Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bafou, and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bafou. Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The skull cult (pah methō mpfō) is at the heart of religious life, together with the traditional court (fə̄m) and the societies ŋgyā ndə́m and ŋkāŋ. • Sacred places: Ndzi'mpfəŋ (at Ndzi'i), Efɔ mə́ŋ lepɛ́ (Balepeh), Efɔ ntoo lefok (Lefok), ŋkuŋkuŋ nda laa (Saa Maya), Nzəm laa (Bameleu), Efɔ shwihi (Ndzenkap). • These sites recall natural phenomena, a hot spring that appeared after a sacrifice, a cave that served as a refuge during the maquis, or a mythical snake with a goatee and a crest. • A birth may mark the return of an ancestor; death leads back to the ancestors. The living consult them in sacred places in times of serious difficulty. • Taboos: incest (sǒk kihi), relations with the wife of the chief or of a notable, murder, adultery, theft, and even eating taro other than with the fingers.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The skull cult (pah methō mpfō) is at the heart of religious life, together with the traditional tribunal (fə̄m) and the societies ŋgyā ndə́m and ŋkāŋ. Sacred places: Ndzi'mpfəŋ (at Ndzi'i), Efɔ mə́ŋ lepɛ́ (Balepeh), Efɔ ntoo lefok (Lefok), ŋkuŋkuŋ nda laa (Saa Maya), Nzəm laa (Bameleu), Efɔ shwihi (Ndzenkap).

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bafou (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Yemba
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.langText: Ǒ zìɛ̀ ndi ? Álā kɛɛ́ lɛ́ ndilefɔ ?
vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bafou and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bafou family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bafou greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bafou family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Yemba. • Greetings: Àtsà’tè = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Ǒ zìɛ̀ ? njhʉ̄ láā ? = morning greeting (one person); Pɛ̌ zìɛ̀ ? njhʉ̄ làā ? = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Wɔ́mɔ’ɔ́, Mépjā, Métɛ̄t, lekwua, Méta:. • Forms of address and titles: ndzi, ŋkem, tɛnyi, mɔ́'ɔ. • The founder, Tɛla' (“the father of the forge”), was renamed Efɔ ndɔŋ (“the chief of horns”) after killing a buffalo and refusing to give its head to the chiefdom of Baleveng.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Yemba are the first steps towards communicating with the Bafou. Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
